ny_new_buck.blurb: A small cliff of about 60 feet in the Lake George Region of the Adirondacks, tucked behind trees and reached by a long woodland walk that ends near a marsh. Its 19 routes are mostly trad with a few bolted lines, and the bulk sit between 5.4 and 5.8, so it suits parties who want plenty of moderates packed close together. A handful of 5.10s and a single 5.11 give stronger climbers something harder. The stone is good quality and carries garnet crystals. Expect bugs in warm weather; it works well as an early-season shakedown outing.

ny_nick_stoner.blurb: The largest block in the Middle Earth boulder cluster at Nine Corner Lake, in the Southern Mountains of the Adirondacks. It holds 19 problems, weighted toward the easy end: five at V0, a spread of V1 to V4, and two hard V7 lines at the top. A low-angled slab section offers gentle climbing, and a big crack splits a narrow face. Most people come down the slab, whose lower edge overhangs a real drop, so descend carefully. From the Troll and Gate boulders, follow the herd path to the right to reach it.

ny_lookout.blurb: A boulder group within the Middle Earth cluster at Nine Corner Lake in the Southern Adirondacks, sitting downhill from the Fortress boulders. Around 18 problems, none harder than V4, with most between V0 and V2 and a good handful of V4s, several of them sit-start variations. That makes it a friendly stop for newer boulderers who still want a few firm tests. A very tall crack runs the full height of the far end of the main block, and a detached pillar stands to the right when you face uphill. From the Troll and Gate boulders, take the herd path rightward; the first big boulders uphill of it are these.

ny_main_cliff_3.blurb: The principal wall of the small Deadwater crag in the Lake Champlain region of the Adirondacks, holding about 18 routes, nearly all trad plus one bolted line. Grades run from 5.6 to 5.12, but most land around 5.9 and 5.10, with a few easier lines and some multi-pitch outings. The wall faces southeast, catching sun from mid to late morning until mid-afternoon. Routes take protection well and finish at their own anchors, but the top is hard to reach without leading, so this is not a top-rope venue. Room at the base is tight apart from one large terrace, so share space with other parties.

ny_hurricane_crag.blurb: A multi-pitch cliff in the Keene area of the Adirondacks, with excellent rock and wide summit views. Most of the 18 routes are trad crack and face lines, running from 5.3 to 5.10 and clustering around 5.8 and 5.9, with a few winter ice and mixed lines added in. It is better known as a summer destination, though sunny winter days suit the shorter cold-weather routes. The climb to the base takes around twenty minutes uphill and passes smaller satellite crags; in winter the route is slower and the trail harder to follow. Pair it with those smaller cliffs for a full day out.
ny_hurricane_crag.approach: A steady uphill walk of about twenty minutes through forest, passing several smaller crags on the way to the main cliff.

ny_peanut_butter_and_jelly_crag.blurb: A cliff of up to about 60 feet on the west side of Pinnacle Mountain, near Caroga Lake in the southern Adirondacks, opposite the better-known Pinnacle Cliff. It holds 18 routes, all trad or top-rope friendly, ranging from 5.3 up to 5.11, with the majority at 5.9 and harder; a few are only 25 to 30 feet tall. A pair of cracks runs top to bottom in the tallest section. Every line finishes at clip-in anchors, reachable by walking around either end, so you can lead or set a top rope. A 60 m rope and a standard rack cover it. Sun arrives in the afternoon.

ny_pebbles_boulders.blurb: A cluster of three large boulders plus a black block just beyond, beside the Undercliff carriage road in the Trapps section of the Gunks. Roughly 17 problems from V0 to V8, mostly in the V0 to V5 range with three at the top end. The blocks are hard conglomerate that has come to rest on its side, so surfaces that were once flat now stand vertical, which gives the climbing an unusual feel. Grades in this part of the Trapps are loose, so treat them as approximate. It is one of the first boulder stops when walking up the road toward Skytop.
ny_pebbles_boulders.approach: From the Trapps bridge, walk about five minutes north along the carriage road, past the Uberfall area toilet; the boulders sit to the left and below the road roughly 200 feet beyond it.
